Beyond
the splat.

Where the tools for 3D video are going—and where a new builder can earn a place.

Gaussian splats have escaped the lab. The next opportunity is making the resulting assets dependable, portable, and economical to deliver.

Jump to the recommendation ↗

Prepared for Teddy · Primary-source research · Approx. 20-minute read

My recommendation: a delivery workbench for 3D video.

Start with an open asset inspector and a paid preflight → profile → package → approve workflow for studios shipping splats into browsers and real-time engines. Specialize in dynamic clips after proving the workflow on static assets. Earn the right to build an encoder from real failures, device measurements, and customer footage.

Conviction: high that Fable understates existing tools; moderate that this is a useful independent product; willingness to pay remains unvalidated. Assumption: a solo founder or small team seeking a credible commercial entry point with room to grow.

01 / CHECK THE PREMISEWhat Fable gets wrong 02 / MAP THE FIELDWhat already exists 03 / FOLLOW THE SCIENCEWhere research is pointing 04 / MAKE THE FIRST MOVEThe product & first 90 days
00

Four different things get called “3D video.”

The distinction changes the customer, bandwidth, capture rig, and feasibility of a product.

Static radiance field

A frozen scene reconstructed from photographs. The camera moves; the scene does not. Spatial streaming fetches nearby detail.

Dynamic / 4D capture

The scene itself changes with time. Playback must preserve motion, temporal consistency, seeking, and usually audio.

Live volumetric video

New observations are captured, reconstructed, encoded, and displayed continuously within an end-to-end latency budget.

Generated worlds & spatial video

Generated 3D, stereo video, and image-to-depth parallax can be useful without recovering a complete, measured, walk-around scene.

A Gaussian splat is an oriented, translucent blob with position, scale, opacity, and appearance. Many overlapping blobs reproduce photographed views without requiring a clean polygon surface. “4DGS” is an umbrella: it can mean independent frame sequences, persistent moving Gaussians, a deformation field, or a time-dependent model. Those are different codec inputs, not interchangeable files. 3DGS foundations ↗

A critical distinction: streaming a precomputed performance is video-on-demand. Rendering that performance at 60 FPS does not establish that it can be reconstructed and broadcast live. Likewise, animating a static splat is not evidence of reconstructing arbitrary motion.

Standards / newly ratified

glTF has crossed a real milestone.

KHR_gaussian_splatting became ratified in the repository on September 3, 2026. The baseline contributor list supports NVIDIA and Cesium/Bentley participation; it does not establish Fable’s Apple/Google attribution. This is a scene representation standard, not an HLS-equivalent 4D media standard.

Ratification commit ↗Contributor announcement ↗
Standards / scene composition

OpenUSD’s ParticleFields have shipped.

OpenUSD 26.03, released February 24, added Gaussian particle fields and a reference renderer. An SPZ converter followed. Renderer hints can still be interpreted differently; a common schema does not ensure identical pixels, temporal behavior, or delivery performance.

03

The research is moving in six directions.

The strongest signal is a shift from isolated scene fitting toward learned geometry, temporal state, deployable representations, and hybrid rendering. A paper result is not a production guarantee.

01 / LEARNED RECONSTRUCTION · 2025–2026

Geometry becomes a reusable model.

VGGT predicts cameras, depth and geometry; AnySplat goes further and emits Gaussians from uncalibrated views. MapAnything supports metric reconstruction across different inputs. These reduce per-scene setup and optimization, but static reconstruction from a moving camera is not automatically moving-scene capture.

VGGT-Omega extends the frontier in 2026; its current code and weights use a noncommercial research license. Original VGGT offers a separate commercial checkpoint, and MapAnything offers an Apache-2.0 model family.

Tool implicationMake model selection replaceable. Capture fidelity, failure diagnosis and consistent outputs are more durable than wrapping one checkpoint.

VGGT / CVPR 2025 ↗AnySplat / SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 ↗MapAnything ↗VGGT-Omega / CVPR 2026 ↗
02 / ONLINE STATE · 2024–2026

Reconstruct the change, preserve history.

3DGStream updates an existing Gaussian scene; Instant Gaussian Stream accelerates updates with learned motion. StreamSplat (Wu et al., ICLR 2026) reports 49ms local runtime per frame on an A100.

The latter is substantial progress, with limitations: pseudo-depth errors, a short deformation window, loss through occlusion, and close-range perspective distortion. It does not establish calibrated, multicamera, networked live capture.

Tool implicationTemporal identity, reset/recovery, calibration drift and p95 latency deserve first-class diagnostics. Rendering FPS alone obscures the system bottleneck.

3DGStream / CVPR 2024 ↗IGS / CVPR 2025 ↗StreamSplat / ICLR 2026 ↗
03 / TEMPORAL COMPRESSION · 2025

Borrow video’s motion and keyframes.

4D-MoDe separates background and moving foreground, predicts motion, and adapts groups of pictures (GOPs). This matches Fable’s motion-decoupling description. It also enables background replacement and foreground-only streaming.

On N3DV, its 11.4KB inter-frame payload excludes a roughly 6,348KB background and 686KB foreground keyframe. Lookahead and per-scene optimization matter. No public implementation was located in this review.

Tool implicationMeasure complete clips, including initialization, keyframes and scene cuts. Persistent object identity is useful for both compression and editing.

4D-MoDe / September 2025 preprint ↗
04 / PROGRESSIVE DELIVERY · 2025–2026

Make partial downloads useful.

LTS demonstrates DASH streaming of multilayer dynamic splats. 4DGCPro uses progressive levels to adapt to bandwidth and device budgets, with reported tablet/desktop playback of 44/58 FPS. PD-4DGS organizes a static scaffold, global motion and local refinement into layers.

Implementation access is the catch: LTS explicitly cannot release its source; 4DGCPro’s linked repo currently contains the project site/data links; PD-4DGS promises noncommercial research code.

Tool implicationProduction implementations still offer room, but start by reproducing a result and securing usable rights. “Compatible with HLS/DASH” does not make a custom splat decoder a native HTML video codec.

LTS / MMSys 2025 ↗4DGCPro / NeurIPS 2025 ↗Linked repository ↗PD-4DGS / May 2026 preprint ↗
05 / HYBRID REPRESENTATIONS · 2025–2026

Meshes, splats and neural appearance coexist.

Neural Harmonic Textures stores learned features and uses deferred neural decoding across different explicit primitives. 3DGRUT explores ray tracing, complex cameras, and integration with other geometry. GeoSplatting connects geometry with physically based inverse rendering.

This points toward hybrid scenes: explicit surfaces for geometry and interaction, radiance for appearance, and learned decoders where useful. It does not prove that splats are about to disappear.

Tool implicationPreserve camera calibration, units, source observations, time, and appearance semantics. A collider mesh and visual splat can be complementary deliverables.

NHT / ECCV 2026 ↗3DGRUT ↗GeoSplatting / ICCV 2025 ↗
06 / PERCEPTUAL QUALITY & CAPTURE · 2025–2026

Human judgment matters beyond PSNR.

GS-QA releases camera-path videos and subjective scores; 3DGS-QA studies native-Gaussian quality prediction. GScomp-QA finds that tested metrics incompletely capture compression artifacts. Next-best-view research selects informative frames from multicamera inputs to improve reconstruction and semantics.

Much evidence still concerns static scenes and bounded datasets. A learned score is not a guarantee against dynamic flicker, disocclusion errors, or failed playback.

Tool implicationCombine explicit acceptance checks, fixed-view comparisons, temporal trajectories and human review. A universal “quality score” should not be the initial product.

GS-QA / QoMEX 2025 ↗3DGS-QA / AAAI 2026 ↗GScomp-QA / May 2026 ↗Dynamic next-best-view ↗

For “live,” insist on the complete clock.

Capture & syncExposure, camera skew, transfer
ReconstructInference, updates, keyframes
Encode & queueRate control, backpressure
Transport & bufferNetwork, loss, ABR
Decode & presentGPU memory, render, display

Measure timestamped capture-to-display latency and throughput separately. Report p50/p95, camera count, resolution, hardware, viewpoint freedom, and failures during motion or occlusion. Parallel stages can improve throughput while queues still increase latency. This is where distributed-systems experience helps—but reconstruction quality and capture hardware remain core dependencies.

Headline resultActual measurementDo not infer
3DGStream: 200 FPSRendering an already reconstructed scene; reconstruction is about 12 seconds per source frame.Live 30 FPS capture. Sequentially, 12s/frame is 360× a 30Hz frame interval. Paper ↗
StreamSplat: 49msAlgorithm runtime including rendering on an A100; approximately 20 frames/s in the measured setting.Phone performance or measured glass-to-glass multicamera latency. Timing table & limitations ↗

These results are deliberately not plotted as a benchmark race: datasets, GPUs, outputs and timing boundaries differ. Numbers above are author-reported; arithmetic conversions are this report’s.

Three plausible futures to design around: captured 4D media delivered locally; mixed mesh/splat/neural scenes with interaction; and action-conditioned generated worlds delivered as pixels. The last may reuse conventional video streaming. Invest in asset acceptance, source history and integration contracts that matter in the first two; do not assume every future world model needs your splat codec. Google’s generated-world direction ↗ Scenarios are analyst inference, not forecasts.
04

Which gaps make good starting wedges?

These are my judgments for a small team, not market-size estimates. The ranking favors a bounded first deliverable, observable customer pain, and manageable research dependencies.

1

Client acceptance & delivery workbench

Help studios prove that a particular asset meets a client’s quality, device, loading and playback requirements.

Why it can work / why it may fail

Can start with existing content and renderers. The risk is that existing vendor tools already solve enough, or failures are too infrequent to sustain subscriptions.

BEST FIRST EXPERIMENT

Research risk: lower
Demand confidence: medium–low
2

Capture QA for one expensive workflow

For a specific rig or use case, find sync, calibration, exposure and coverage defects before a reshoot becomes costly.

Tradeoff

Clear economic event: a bad capture. Requires access to raw cameras/data and differentiation from SplatKing, Mavericks and existing capture previews.

BEST WITH A CAPTURE PARTNER

Research risk: medium
3

Open 4D packaging & streaming tools

A maintained command-line encoder/segmenter and reference player for a precisely defined temporal representation.

Tradeoff

Excellent open-source learning path. Commercially, Gracia/Evercoast and emerging open code raise the bar. Need a measured advantage in cost, portability or reliability.

BEST AMBITIOUS OSS BET

Research risk: high
4

A narrow dynamic finishing tool

For example, maintain a performer mask through time and export a stable foreground into one production engine.

Tradeoff

Artists understand the task. Temporal coherence and lighting are hard, and incumbent editors are adding features. Start as a plugin with a committed studio.

BEST WITH ARTIST ACCESS

Research risk: high
5

General reconstruction orchestration

Versioned GPU jobs, retries, storage and reproducible research environments.

Tradeoff

Useful infrastructure, but cloud offerings, AWS guidance and packaged trainers reduce differentiation. Make it an implementation detail of a valuable workflow.

SUPPORTING CAPABILITY

Standalone moat: weak

A full live sports or concert platform ranks poorly as a first solo project: synchronized capture, occlusion, real-time reconstruction, distribution, production operations and content access must all work together. That can become a company, but it requires a committed capture/customer partner and more than a codec.

05

Build around the handoff.

The first buyer hypothesis: a technical director or lead developer at a capture studio or interactive agency, delivering client assets into a browser or real-time engine.

“Will this asset work for this client?”

Turn a splat export into a measured, reviewable delivery: show the failures along the intended camera path, compare export options, and produce the package that meets the agreed device and quality budget.

Concrete trigger

The workstation preview looks fine.

The client opens the same asset on a phone and sees stalls, missing detail, color differences, or an out-of-memory failure. The studio has to determine whether the capture, export, compression or player is responsible.

Proposed result: one review link tying an exact source and export version to repeatable camera paths, annotated visual defects, device measurements, and an accepted delivery profile.

This scenario is a product hypothesis grounded in documented rendering/memory/format friction. It is not a customer interview result.

Differentiation to prove

Resolve failures across vendor boundaries.

Basic file statistics, reconstruction metrics and job queues already exist. The useful product combines them with actual end-user playback, visual comparison, client approval, and an explanation of what to change.

Build adapters to existing tooling. A bug corpus, regression history and repeated acceptance workflow could become defensible assets; a generic “splat validator” is easy for incumbents to bundle.

Existing validation ↗Existing regressions ↗Services competitor ↗
01 / INSPECT

Source & assumptions

Inspect schema and any declared units, up-axis, SH/color conventions and timestamps. Preserve originals and record explicit transforms. Flag missing metadata and unknown conventions.

02 / COMPARE

Exports & playback

Render identical views in selected runtimes. Measure first useful view, frame-time percentiles, bytes and failures on real devices.

03 / REVIEW

Visual acceptance

Annotate floaters, missing coverage and flicker on a fixed path. Separate capture defects from regressions introduced downstream.

04 / DELIVER

Package & history

Publish through an existing player, keep the tested profile, record acceptance, and re-run checks after a pipeline update.

Keep the first implementation small.

Choose one production route—for example, a supported PLY export through SplatTransform into PlayCanvas—and compare a subset of the same assets in Spark to expose renderer differences. Support a fixed camera envelope and two real target devices chosen by a design partner. Begin with static content because it is readily available; add one explicit dynamic representation when a partner provides repeat business.

Dynamic support adds timestamps and audio alignment, temporal identity or births/deaths, startup to the first moving frame, seeking, keyframe spikes, and quality under changing bandwidth. A codec adapter must declare these capabilities and refuse unsupported conversions. A variable-topology PLY sequence should not silently enter a codec that requires persistent point indices.

# Proposed interface — product sketch, not an implemented tool splat-check inspect source.ply --profile client-web splat-check compare delivery-manifest.json --path approved-tour.json splat-check report run-id --include-device-results
Business model to test: open CLI and fixtures; paid project/device runs, review history, team approvals and pipeline integrations. Start by charging for a delivery audit and repair plan. For discovery, test a $750–$1,500 fixed-scope pilot; that is a proposed experiment, not an observed market price. Move to subscriptions only when partners repeatedly need the workflow.

Delivery economics create a measurable constraint.

Evercoast publicly lists splat examples at 75–182 Mbps and bandwidth starting at $0.35/GB. Those are vendor examples and pricing, not a universal bitrate or minimum cost. They are useful inputs for testing whether an experience is viable. A compression improvement has value only if it preserves the required views and can decode on the target device. Example bitrates ↗ Current published pricing ↗

What does a completed view cost?

Change the assumptions. Defaults illustrate a 10-minute clip at 75Mbps and 1,000 complete views.

ILLUSTRATIVE BANDWIDTH BILL
$1,969
5.63 GBper completed view
5,625 GBtotal delivered

Decimal GB = Mbps × seconds ÷ 8,000. Cost = GB × views × price/GB. Excludes capture, reconstruction, encoding, storage, requests, audio, retries and discounts. Real adaptive playback varies by viewpoint and device; use average delivered bitrate. This is arithmetic, not a vendor quote.

06

The first 90 days should buy evidence.

Do not spend the first quarter designing a universal container. Learn enough graphics to diagnose real assets, then find a repeatable job a customer will pay to finish.

DAYS 01–14

Learn one complete path.

Reconstruct one small static scene with Brush or gsplat, edit it in SuperSplat, publish in PlayCanvas and Spark. Inspect splat attributes and rendering differences. Run one licensed dynamic example with an existing player.

Interview 12–15 studios/integrators. Ask for their last rejected delivery, hours spent diagnosing it, target devices, and whether they can share a representative failing asset.

Gate: at least three partners contribute real assets and concrete acceptance requirements. If nobody can name repeated costly failures, revisit the wedge.
DAYS 15–45

Deliver audits manually.

Evaluate about 20 assets from those partners. Automate only the repeated steps: imports, reference paths, export comparisons, device measurements and annotated reports.

Test paid audits. Record operator time before/after, the cause of every failure, and whether the client actually accepts the resulting package. Include a midrange phone, not just a research GPU.

Gate: two paid pilots and a recurring failure pattern that existing tools do not resolve easily. A target of 50% less diagnostic/review time is a hypothesis to measure.
DAYS 46–90

Productize the repeated job.

Release the small CLI and useful fixtures. Add stored baselines, review links and one pipeline integration. Introduce dynamic timing/seek checks only with customer clips.

Benchmark an existing open 4D format against the client’s incumbent route. Decide whether a missing encoder feature, better scheduling or better diagnosis creates the biggest improvement.

Gate: partners return with another project and pay again. Build a codec only if measured capability or economics force it; otherwise keep using existing components.
What would change my recommendation

Follow unusually strong access.

If you already have a synchronized capture partner and committed live telepresence customer, start with capture-to-browser measurement and synchronization. If your goal is mainly research learning, contribute to an open 4D encoder/player immediately. If an artist has a painful finishing task and will pay, build that plugin.

The general recommendation assumes those advantages are not yet established.

Kill or narrow the idea when

The handoff is not a recurring problem.

Stop if existing exporters/player tools solve most issues, studios will not supply representative assets, manual support dominates every job, or project frequency cannot support recurring revenue. Also narrow scope if each “4D” input needs its own research project.

Open-source popularity, beautiful demos, and benchmark wins are learning signals. They are not substitutes for repeat paid use.

If you pursue Fable’s encoder + segmenter + player wedge, scope it this way.

Start with prerecorded clips from one reconstruction system, one declared temporal model, and one browser/device pair. Baseline Gracia/Evercoast where accessible and splats4D where compatible. Measure complete clip bytes, first dynamic frame, seek latency, p95 frame time, memory residency where instrumentation permits, and visual errors during cuts/occlusion.

Reuse existing image/video decoding where a representation supports it. Define how decoder configuration, timestamps, keyframes, random access and audio map into segments. Add adaptive streaming only after basic playback is robust. Keep a live pipeline as a later milestone: first demonstrate measured capture-to-display latency on a real synchronized rig.

Winning claim to earn: “For this capture type and these devices, we meet the same acceptance quality with lower delivery cost or fewer integration failures.” A generic claim that streaming does not exist is already untenable.

Implementation diligence: licenses, reference renders, and what a standard does not solve.

The original INRIA implementation has a noncommercial research/evaluation license. gsplat and 3DGRUT identify Apache-2.0 licenses; Brush is Apache-2.0 and PlayCanvas tools are MIT. Code, pretrained weights, dependencies and example footage can have different terms. Publicly visible code is not necessarily reusable in a paid product.

Use the ratified glTF baseline and released OpenUSD schema where appropriate. Record appearance conventions and the intended rendering behavior, then compare actual images. Neither standard removes the need to define temporal topology, frame dependencies, audio timing or decoder requirements.

INRIA license ↗ · gsplat ↗ · VGGT-Omega weight/code terms ↗ · glTF semantics ↗

Make one studio’s next 3D delivery predictable. That is a practical way to learn the field, find a buyer, and discover which piece of the future stack deserves to become a company.

07

Sources, scope, and confidence.

Checked 8 September 2026. Citations next to each claim link directly to primary material. These starting points make the report easier to revisit as the ecosystem changes.

What is evidenced

Existence and documented scope.

Official products, SDK artifacts, repository contents, release dates, papers and author demonstrations. Named absence claims were actively tested with counterexamples.

What is not measured here

Independent product performance.

No reconstruction benchmarks, paid vendor trials, physical-device player tests or customer interviews were performed. Embedded demos illustrate claims; they are not reproduced experiments.

What is a judgment

The commercial opening.

The recommendation, ranking, pilot pricing and milestones are analyst hypotheses. “Not located” describes this search, not proof that no competing tool exists.
